div.p: TDE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 5, 1889.
FEARFUL MURDER IN BRADFORD.- HORRIBLE MUTILATION OF A BOY.

The epidemic of murder and mutilation which has sensed consternation in the Eat End of London has at length broken out in the provinces, and, although the crime dboovered on Saturday morning at Bradford hes I from the methods of the aneassin and the sex of the victim apparently no direct connection with the White- chapel outrages, there can be little doubt that the mind of the culprit has been strongly influenced by the recent II occurrenem le the MetrapnHA The problem of motive is if pewit"' et, more difficult of solution in this owe than in the ease of the murdered unfortunates. A cheerful, inoffensive 104, of respectable parentage. strikes upon intimery with the fsmily milkman. One morning the boy leaves him, between seven and sight o'clock for the purpose of accomnanying the milkman on his rounds, circumstance which arouses no comment, an it has frequently happened before. According to the milkmen, the her parts compeny with him just before the last call is made, and proceeds in the directian him mother's house, which is then about 200 yards distant. The mother, however, never mem her eon alive attain, but exactly 48 hours after the lad left his home, his body. mutilated in a most horrible manner, is discovered within a stone throw of his metrer's residency. As far as ran be seen it is impossible that the tragedy *add beve been prompted by env feelings of revenge aeainst either the hen or his parents. The name of the mur- , tiered boo was John Gill. He was eight years of age, smart, bright, and intelligent almost beyond hie rem. and with his whoolfellows wag extremely popular. Ms hithei, a catr'river, well known and respected in I Bradford, lives in Thorneliffe-rnad. a thoroughfare running, from Manninghamidene, the chie4 resi- dential district of the town, to the Midland Railway, and it mm in a heck street opening out of Thorn- cliffe-road that his son's remains were found.

On Thursday morning, John told hie mother that he was going for a ride with Barrett, a milk- man who serves families In thb nett of Bradford. Mrs. Gill knevr that her son was on friendly terms with Barrett and was in thy habit of going with him to the Aim:lent railway station to fetch hi, mint and she thought nothing of fits incident. Johnny waited at, the door until Barrett palmed on his way to the station. which was at 7 30, when he climbed info the cart and went off. Independent witnesses lum come forward to Mate that they saw the hay with Barrett at the railway station and also subsequonilr, whilst the milk W. being delivered at the customers' houses. In fart, Barrett hinmelf adnaits that Johnny remained with him until all the calla but one had been made. When the else drew np at Walter Villas, whem ho last customer reside& the bey, Barrett affirrne,junmed down, and mid he would run , home and get his brmkfast. As has alreudy been ! anted, the Any then disappeared for two days. Finding he ! ! did not retorn for his morning meal, his mother made in- , ! utilities amongst the neighbeurs, but to no avail. Nobody ' hed seen orlward anything of him from theamment he was alleged to have let t the milkmen. On Friday morning, no trace of the missing lad haying been found, the fol- lowing atlyortisement was inserted inn tonal nowatuper "Lone, on Thuraday morning, boy. John Gill. aged eight; was last men sliding in Walmer Villas at 830 a.m.; had on navy blue ton root (with brass buttons on)), mid. shietnanb cap. plaid knickerbockers, laced hems, red end black atockinga; complexion tale; home, 41, Thorn- eliffe-rood." The day passed without any slim et the it. and Mr. and Mrs. Gill retired to reet on Friday night wMI nigh distracted with apprettention. Mrs. Gill did not me anything of Barrett from the time that Johnny left with him on Thuraday morning until about three o'clock the same afternoon, when in reply to her quiet' dons he said (ho boy loft him while hut start wag at Weimer Villas. He also mated that Johnny was sliding as he ran down Thorneliffe-street. On Friday morning. Barrett again called on the Gals to ask if any tidings had been heard of the boy. _

The discovery of the dead body eras node st 7 30 on Paturday morning by a youth timed Jew. 8.., who arts as stableman for Mr. Berwick, a butcher, renting uertain outbuildings in Mehoestreet, near Theencliffes wad. div.head: TREAT TO AGED PEOPLE IT WARRINGTON. _
div.p: TREAT TO AGED PEOPLE IT WARRINGTON. _

On Thursday a number of the aged poor 01 the town were feasted at the Public Hall. in accordance with a custom that has been observed annually in Warrington for many year.. At noon the old men Pe down to dinner, and in the after- noon the aged women had tea. Particulars are appended. THE OLD MEN'S DINNER. . .

_ ..... A substantial dinner was provided for the old men, each of the guests being over 80 )-ears of age. The met, an ueurel, WM defrayed by public subscription. Antonget the men present were 271, whose ogee ranged from 40! to 89 years, 58 from 70 to 78 pars of age, and 23 from ! 77 to 84 veers of age. Several dinners were abso mint out tol thosewno, owing to infirmity, wereunable to leave home. ! The fare consisted of roast beef, boiled and roast legs ' of mutton, nut pork, rabbit Moe vegetables, cheese and beer. After the repast those of the guests who were partial to "the weed " wane supplied with tobaece. The president of the Aged People's Treat Committee is Councillor John Pierpoint ; bon. secretary, the Mayor (Alderman Siitton)e hon. treuurer, Mr. Thomas Morris; vice-president, Mr. Thomas Jones ; ! while the other membersof the. taammittee are Mesers. J. E. Wright, Samuel Jones, W. J. Horton, Charles Skinner, Peter Caldwell, James Smethuat, Peter eltrimee, D. Fanshaw, and Daniel Jones. In addition to the above gentlemen nest of whom were present, there were also in attendance the Rev. S. and Mrs. Wilkinson, Mesdames Sutton (Mayorese), Pierpoint, Harriun, ClarieCarletun, Wray. Chrinies, % enn,Wright, Horton It. T. Smith, Fmneomb, and the Misses Aliton:Griffiths, Walker, Wood, Rankin, Chrimu, and Jackson ;the Rev. J. Iland,Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, arid Messrs. George Riley, J. Walker, D. Rankin T. Dorn- ville (who collected the tickets), Hannah, Dooley, Dowd, J. H. Smethurst, Howard, Pitt, ft. Allbis, Orifn hs, Litton, and J. Chrirnee, jun., many el whom waited upon the old men during their dinner. The meal was excellently cooked by Mrs. Shackleton and her aesietants. During the time that the men were !partaking of It Mr. W. S Woods played selections of music ou the organ. After the appetites of all had been satisfied, Councillor John Pienuint wished all present a very happy New Year. leo doubt, he raid, some who were present last year weni also present now, and it night also be expected that some, on account isf their age, were no longer with them. He asked them to drink two toasts together, to save time, namely, "The health of the Queen" and "the Prince and Princess of 1 Wales and the rest of the Royal Family."—The Hee. S. Wilkineon next spoke. He said he would Ville* in the footsteps of the President, and wish all present e A , happy New You," in the highest some of the word. He believed that the son woo beginning to shine through the clouds at Warrington. He was told on every handl that trade was reviving, and although perhaps many in that room were not able to do much work themselves. if 1 trade revived in Warrington he hoped they and the rest ! Of the public would reap the benefit of it. (Hear, hear.) He wee glad that the first toast which had been pro. posed was that of the Queen, and to hear the hearty response which was given to the call of the Chairman furl three cheers for her Majesty, bemuse it showed that they were all loyal citirons. The Bible distinctly told them that their duty was to "Pear God and honour the Ring." They were living under a monarch who set them a good example in every way, and who was a good and kind-hearted Christian. (Applause.) He was glad they had commenced the year by meeting together at a Andal gatlwring, because lie bdb...,1 that an excellent dinner brought out all the good qualities of an Englishman ; and looking round the table he thought all the men present were at that moment at peace with the world.—Mr. Pierpoint said there was another toast which must not be forgotteu, and it was the health of the subscrilurs to the treat. The old M.ll knew that they were indebted to the charity of a number of . liberally disposed ladies and gentlemeu of the town and neighbourhood for the excellent dinner they ! had just enjoyed, and it was their duty to show their appreciation of the kilidnea, which had been extended !to them in the manner he had suggested. He had the , honour to be the president of the Treat Committee, and [he could aseure them that there was no decrease in the number of those who had been provided with a dinner Ithat day. As msny old men had been present that day , Reeve... and he was pleased to see them looking so well. ! Each ticket of admission contained the mine of the old man to be supplied with dinner, as well as les age and ! address, and lie mentioned that fact for the benefit of !the public. Having given some information with 1 reference to the ages of the men present, Mr. Pierpoint I concluded by :edam the commny to drink to the health of the subscribers. The toast was warmly received, and a tong having been given by one of the men—Mr. Jeroph 'Warburton, who is 82 years of age—the National Anthem was sung, and the proceediugs were brought to a close.

div.p: AGED WOMEN'S. TFA •

in the evening—crose on 450 aged women of the town partook of a substantial tea, in the Public Hall. The tables were again attended to by the ladies and gentle- men who were present in the afternoon, in addition to whom there were also present Councillor Fleming,lfrs. It. W. Collin, Mrs. Anton, Miss Roberts, Mr. John Harrison. Them being no many aged people present the plat- form as well as the body of the hall, had to be utilised for seating space. After tea an admirable entertainment was given at which there were present, in addition to the old people, a large number of ticket holders who com- pletely filled the gallery. The chair was taken by Coon- calor John Pierpoint, who was supported by the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), the Rev. S. Wilkin- son, Rev. J. E. Hand, Messrs. T. Morris, D. Jones, J. Smethurst, P. Chrimes, J. E. Wright and others. The CHAMMAN said they were all glad to see so many of the old denten present again that night. They were all aware that one or two or more had departed this life since that gathering was last held. One poor old woman they would all recollect, whose name woe Sarah Ifirchall, and who had liven to be upwards of 100 years of age. (Hear, hear.) He might tell them that through the kindness of a member of their Committee—Mr. James Smethurst—the old dame, though in low and poor circumstances, was respectably buried. ((lear, hear.) Mr. Pierpoint then wished the aged people a happy new year, and expressed the hope that they would all be there next year to partake of the bounties they had enjoys' that evening. (Applause.) The Rev. S. Witamsox said they must all thank the Cointnittee and other ladies and gentlemen who had helped to get up that gathering, and he concluded with noose suitable ads-ice • o those present. The Mason referred to the services rendered by the various members of the Committee, and to the loss they had sustained by the death of the late Mr. Noah Legge. Mr. David Fanshaw, of Whitecross, had, he said, been appointed to succeed Mr. Legge, and they believed that gentleman would prove a useful membet of he Committee. With regard lathe treat fund he said that at the commencement of the year 1887 they had a balance in hand of £6O, out of which in June of that year thvy paid towards the jubilee treat to the aged poor the sum of £23. so that they were left with , a balance of £37. They get in subscriptions, be., £BO Bs. DI., making a total of £ll7 On. 2d. The Cot of their entertainment last year amounted to £9O 75., thus having them with a balance in the 'busk of £27 Is. 2d. They had got to add to that the subscriptions of last year to meet the expenses of the treats of that day. The number of old people, that were treated went on increasing year IT year and they requinsl more funds now than formerly, no that he hoped the public of Warrington would in future help them all they possibly could. (Ilear, hear, and applause.) The Custom,: said that in the afternoon there were 352 old men served with dinners, exclusive of eight or ten that were sent out. That night 445 old woman had sat down to tea. One of them was 89 years of age, two 86, two 84, one 82. one 81, three 80, three 79, one 78, five 76, two 77; twenty others over 70, and the remainder between 60 and 70.

Mr. T. Moant also addressed a few words to the people pratont, and afterwards the musical part of the pmgramme was proceeded with. The programme was admirably carried out by the arti*tes whose names ' appeared upon it, viz.: Mi. Cavanagh, Mr. Cavanagh, Mr. Mamie. and Mr. Littlewood, the t!ornic .ngs and sketches of Mr. Antonio being particularly appreciated. Mr. George Riley officiated as accompanist.

div.head: POLICE COURT PROCEEDINGS.-111PORTANT
div.p: POLICE COURT PROCEEDINGS.-111PORTANT
EVIDENCE.

At the Bradford Borough Police Come on Welneeday William Barrett, milkman, 23, was again brought up la custody oo suspicion of having murdered the boy Gill. Yr. Armitage presided, and there was • full attendance of magistrates. It having become known that import- ant evidence would be given, great public Interest was evinced in the ease, and many people were unable to obtain admission to the court. Prisoner on entering the dock displayed remarkable aoseasleser, but as the day wore on and new facts were disclosed his demeanour underwent considerable alteration, and during the after- noon he Yams' as for forward as possible and followed the evidence with eager attention. Mr. Withers, chief constable, conducted the ease on behalf of the police ; Mr Craven, solicitor, appeared for the prisoner ; and Mr. Freeman, solicitor, watched the proceedings on behalf of the relatives of the deceased. Mr. Withers, in his opening statement, briefly recapi- tulated .he circumstances under which the boy left home on Thumelay morning, and then proceeded to give an nutlins• of the new evidence which heproposed tosubmit. He said witnesses would be called to prove that the boy was in Barrett's cart after the time prisoner said he left him. It was a peculiar thing that prior to the morning in question the boy had never gone home to breakfast when he had been round with Barrett. It seemed odd that he should have done so on Thursday. A witness would be called whowould state pcoitively that Gill deliverol milk at her house for Barrett shortly before ten o'clock that morning, and three persons would rime forward and state that they had seen Barrett with deceased after I 8.30, when prisoner said the boy left him. It would be proved that, although the prisoner said he did not leave home between ten on Thursday night and seven on Friday morning, he was seen walking from his house in the direction of Isis stable at 5.3000 Friday morning. Another witness would swear that there was a light in the stable at 8.25. OnFriday evening Mrs. Gill met the prisoner and asked if he knew where her boy was. She added, " You will have to know, for the detectives are coming up in the morning, and you will have to tell them won. thing." The prisoner replied, " All right," and walked away. A draper who passed the stable on his way home would prove that there was a light in the building at eleven o'clock that night, and another witness who lived at the Servant's Ilome, at the back of the stable, would give important evidence respecting noises she heard dur- ing the same night. At 8 30 on :Saturday morning Barrett called on Mrs. Gill, and it would be shown that he was then going towards home, and not coming from it,as might have been expected. In coming down the street, moreover, the prisoner must have passed within forty yards of the spot where the body was found an hour later. The state of deceased's clothes was sufficient to show that lie was not inurdered in the street. tut in mime building. Three pieces of textile fabric had been discovered in the stables, and in one cAse at least the borough analyst found that stains thereon were the Iseult of blood. The most serious part of the ease was the question of motive, and in this connection the nature of the mutilation was a matter which was very material. On the evidence which he had indicated he proposed to ask fora remand for a week... .

Viltneases having been called to describe the move. ments of the prisoner and the boy in company on Thursday morning as far as Walmer-villaa, Mire Nellie Pearson, of Bertram-rd., owner that she ; took in the milk from a little boy, whotn she had hien- ; tilted as deceased, as late af3 ten minutes to ten. The ; milkman Barrett was standing by his horse's head in front of the gate. Bertha Pickard, schoolgirl, of 10, Church-et., Man- ningliani, 13 years of age, deposed to seeing the prisoner on Thursday morning about 10 o'clock in the back of Bertram-road. Constable Kirk said he examined the exact spot where the body was found four times between 10.25 on Friday night and 4.25 on Saturday morning and raw nothing. Lisaie Jefferson, servant at the Servants Home, No 13., _ . . .

Belle Toe, said that opposite the backyard of No 11 there was a stable occupied by Mr. W.olfenden, dairy. man, Manning/lam-lane. There was a window in this stable which looked towards their scullery window. The lower part of the stable window was made up of "

wood, anirthe upper part was of glass. Witness re-Jettts breed the morning of Friday, the 28th December. She got up that morning at half-past flee o'clock, and wets for some time engaged in the kitchen. Between twenty- fire minutes and half-past six o'clock she went into the scullery.—The Chief Countable—When you went into the scullery did you observe anything P—The witness I saw a light in the stable.—Had you ever seen a light in the stable as early as that before ?—No, sir.—Did you see the prisoner that morning ?—No, sir. Benjamin Abbott, draper, of Manningham-lane, said that on Friday night he was going home about a quarter or ten minutes to eleven, and no he was passing up the back of Belle Vice a light in the stable attracted his attention. lie thought lie had seen a light there on previous evenings. Mr. Craven.—You are not altogether certain as to when you now the light on the occapian previous to Friday 2—Witness No, I am not altogether certain whether it might be on the Thursday or the Wednesday night. I should not like to say. Eliza Jane Kendall, matron of the Servanta' Home, Belle Vue, mid—There is a stable at the back of the Home, which h occupied by Mr. Wolfenden, of the Ashfield Dairy. I know ?Jr. Wolfenden's man, the pri- soner, by seeing him going in and out of the stable. On Saturday morning last, between one and three o'clnek, I heard IL noise proceeding Donn the stable. I heard a continuous rubbing,or rubbing backwards and forwards. —Can you give us any further description do not think lean. I sat up in bed and heard it continually and listened very attentively.—For how long did the noise continue ?—I should think it was going on for about eight or ten minutes.—What was the noise like?— It was like a brushing or scraping, or a noise similar to that of swilling. Witness con- tinued I listened to it until I could hear nothing more, but I still sat up in bed. When the noise had ceased and I was still sitting up when I hoard mine footsteps come out and walk quickly down, past our card door, towards Manningliam-lane.-Did you hear anything else ? —I thought I heard a door shut, but I won't he positive, as lam positive of everything else I have told you. I got op about eight o'clock and made a communication too person named Agnes Brooksbank, who was sitting by me at breakfast time. At that time I had not heard of the murder. Constable Firth stated that on Saturday, while he was in charge of the prisoner at the Town Hall, Barrett mid the sister of John Gill had been with him several times to the station for Milk, but having read about the out- rages on girls he would not have hor with hini any more, and sent her away from the cart many times Detective-efficer King stated that on Saturday morning he visited Barrett's 'IOUS, He made a search and found a bread knife, width had been reccntly cleaned. At Wolfenden's stable he found a wrapper. A portion of the stable between the water tap and the sink was very wet, RS though recently swilled.—The witnees wan proceeding to say that the prisoner had betm questioncil with regard to the cloth, when the magistrate' clerk, interposing, said the statement was not evidence, as the

div.p: THE ENGISEER's STATEMENT.

Is leSt.t, while irtagage-d as engineer of the steamship Evelyn, hound for Constantinople, 1 first found that 1 was sot a healthy man," says Mr. William Murphy, of 1, Ileorge Street, Cork. "1 had severe pains in the small of my back; my head ached almost constantly; and I began to lose appetite and energy. When I had finished the ' voyage and returned to Cork, I I.allvd on one of the very best medical practitioners in the city, but us! found I was receiving no benefit tenon stopped his attendance. By this time I had become very greatly 'weakened ; eould scarcely walk, weak pulse, furred' tongue. Ind taste in the mouth, appetite almest entirely gone,greatest difficulty in retaining the simplmt kind of nourishment on the stomach, and the old pains in the head and back were increased threefold. One day I pickni up, quite accidentally, &canths bed, where nty little niece had left it, a book in which• my cane wax most accurately deecribed, and at the 'tame time giving instances of such cases being coned by 'Warners than Cunt.' The Christmas number of The Queen" is a very strong productim There is a beautiful coloured supple- ment "My Lady Sledging," and there is a large number of full-page illustrations. The fmshion designs are legion ; and, beyond all, there are seasonable articles of high-class. The paper on "English Poetesses," by Osear Wilde, is in his taut style. Me h se.% will find much to intereA them in "The Queen;' The first part is to hand of a new serial production hir Messrs. Cassell anti Co.—. The Story of the Heavens.. It is front the pen of Sir Robert S. Itall,Reyal Astronomer of Ireland. It is a noble subject, nobly treated. With the first part, a star temp is presented; Rhine been care- fully prepared, as it most clearly indicates the various constellations. The work is likely to prove very popuLlis as It is written in an attractive style, and is amply illustrated. Full particulars are also printed of several new special Prirc Competitions for 1889, in which a large nem.er of valuable prizes and medals are offered. HOUGHTON ; I Stipp,se trade must be improving.—Mr. lbacsacity Yes, it is. THR HOUSR COMISITTN6.—THR GUARDIANS ARM ASION-110Dien PAUPERS. The House Committee recommended that in future relatives and blend:, of inmates of the Work- houu, when visiting, should not be allowed to take into the Workhouse baskets and bags, but leave ! them at the lodge. Mr. VOMRT, in loosing the confirmation of the minutes, said that at the meeting of ! the Committee the Master or Matron tort properly brought to the notice of the Committee that (here were in the House certain able-bodied paupers, who, in their I opinion, ought not to be there. One of these men, earned Hopwood, was in the Workhouse with his wife and four children, and another was named Connor, whose wife and two children were also in the House. He was perfectly sure that both these men ought to be brought before the Board. Ile thought that Connor was physically able to do any amount of work which might be given to him, as he looked to be one of the strongest men in Warrington. He had been allowed out seve- ral times to seek for employment, but he had never got it and always returned. He was of opinion that men like these ought not to be there, as they were simply making a convenience of the work- house. Mr. Voii:ey then mentioned the names of Fair- hurst, Pemberton, Miskell, Bate, and Wilkinson as those of able-bodied inmates —Mr. RATCLITTR said the only way to keep these men out of the workhouse was to give them increatted lalsmr.—The CEWGE said that the mane Miskell hadlost ihrecfingers,and theomsequemy wasthat when he was sent to goal he could not be put to hard labour, so that, in fact, he was no worse in goal than there. —The Woasuocss Mast-am—He says lie is better eft. (Lauglirer.)—TheCLEGHthought that thebest plan would, perhaps, be In give these Men tasks they were competent to perform, and if they did not perform those tasks they could be sent to goal—later on in the proceedings, the two men, Connor and Hopwood, were called into the Board room, and the Chairman spoke to them of the desirability of their getting work outsicle.—CoNyokt asked if a man was togs out to rob and plunder or go to gaol. He was a man who spoke for himself. He had a wife and family in that workhouse, and had no place to take thon to outside. Ile had neither friends nor relatives outside, and was he to take his wife and children out into the streets to be " clowned. with cold and hunger. Connor then went on to say that if the Guardians would allow him sufficient to keep him a week he would take out Ids wife and family and seek work, and, at any rate, he would not return to that workhouse. The Board agreed that Connor should be allowed togs out lees week to seek work, leaving his wife and children in the workhouse. It was also pointed out that the Guardians could not supply him with money or with new clothes for which he asked. With regard to the other cases the Workhouse Master was instructed to give them a vigilant supervision. div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. JANUARY 5. 1889.
" VACCINATION by Act of Parliament " is the title of a vigc mom article in the Independent Sec- tion.of the January number of "The Westminster
Review: The writer is evidently familiar with

every phase of the controversy that has been excited as to the wisdom or unwisdom of compul- sory vaccination ; and it is obvious that he has made up his mind that compulsion is not only unnecessary but harmful. We are among those who are of opinion that the balance of evidence is strongly in favour at vaccination ; but we do not on that account wish to stifle discussion. We rather agree with the " Lancet," which a year ago said: "It is too often the custom to think that the question is not worth reasoning or investiga- ting further lint in the present day people think for themselves, and often intelligently so, on medical matters.- This much is certain, that if the case for vaccination is well fouuded, it will not be shaken by dispassionate discus- siou, The writer in "Theo Westminster" takes pains to show that nobody in these diva holds to the original opinion that vaccination is an absolute safeguard against small-pox. Granted that this is so, it does not by any means follow that vacein- athal is of no value, or that the State is not justi- lied, on recognising its eflicury in mitigating disease, in enforcing the compulsion. It is more to the purpose to quote authorities, and supply evidence tosuggest that the State is leaning on a weak if not a broken reed. It is regarded as significant that Dr. CHARLES CREIWITON, the writer of the article on Vaccination in the new edition of the " Encyclopiedia Britannica ' Isis been led to change his opinion upon the subject, and that lie is not now hi hanstblly in his views with the majority of his medical brethren. Ile is riot, to be sure, elone in thinking the sulject requires further elucida- tion, for severe! years ago Sir ANnicew CLsaa, the President of the Royal College of Surgeons, stated thlt—. Compulsory or non-com- pulsory vacci nation was among the most import- ant questions engaging the attention of thoughtful men.- Speaking at a meeting of the Metropolitan Asylum Boardhold in 1880, Sir E. H. Celtics, the chairman, urged the expenditure of £116,000 for additional small-pox hospital accommodation. He said "As sure as you are in this room, there is certain to be a small-pox epidemic in the metropolis at no distant date. It always comes round with the greatest regularity." Now why,it is pertinent to ask, should it always coins round with the greatest regularity, when compulsory vaocination is in full swing The answer of many medical inen is that it is because vaccination afforda protection for a time only, and that there meat be re-vaccination every seven years to secure an, immunity from epidemics. On the other hand there are some intelligentobeervers, like the writer in "The Westminster," who have little or no faith in vaccination, said their contention is that, with the recurrence of small-pox epidemics, the case for compulsion breaks down. Another point which is much debated is whether vaccination is the means of inflicting injury, apart from the question as to whether it is any security against small-pox. The new year has been ushered in with quite a shower of knighthoods; and yet nobody seems one penny the worse.
There was a total eclipse of the son on New Year's Day, which was quite visible at the house of friend Jones. HIE wife presented him with twin daughters, and the son was for the time snuffed out.
' Sir Charles and Lady Mike are making the most of their visit to India. They ore both observant travellers, and they will both have something valuable to say on their return to England.

Th.. I.,u,nopolists are at work. Notice has been m an advance of twenty per cent in the price of salt. If this sort of thing goes on, the monopo_ . lists will have to be dealt with; there is a limit to ' the patience of the mot patient of people.

The cry has arisen that our ships are short of guns, and our cavalry short of horses. Query: Where does the money go? The question ought to be answered, and, if need be, somebody ought to be sacked. It is well for us that we are, just at present, short, too, of enemies.

This messenger left Omdurman on the 2:lrd November, and, if his tale is to be b.ilieved, Emin is safe, neil, persumably, Stanley is safe too.

The whole subject, we cannot but think, requires further investigation. LIBERAL. owe much YO the late JOHN STUART MILL, and they scarcely know as yet the extent of their indebtedness to him, for never a year passes but some of the truths of which he was the prophet secure further recognition and acaeptanca lie was laughed at by unthinking people as a man possessed of a foolish crotchet when he seriously argued, in the House of Commons, that the franchise ought to be extended to the female tax- payer as well as to the male; but the seed which he sowed in this particular plot took root, and has brought forth a hundred-fold, Women are per- mitted to vote in Municipal, School Board, and Board of Gimrdians elections; and now within the last six inonthswe have had the PRIME MINISTER laffirming that there is no good reason why women should not be allowed to vote in Parliamentary elections. We are in the thick of an Irish agitation, and are likely to be for some time. Home Rule is in the air; it is a new thing to many, and Mr. GLAIATONE has been denounced for taking up with it as a new thing; but Joins STUART Mni. discussed Home Rule with Mr. JOHN Moe- LEN in 1873. Some time before his death, he was on a visit to Mr. MORLEY for a single day, and the latter, in an article which he wrote in the "Fortnightly Review," mentions Home Rule as one of the subjects they "spoke of" whilst together. It might, of course, be suggested that this conveys ,nothing as to MILLS'S views on Ire- land; but those who are familiar with the works of the great political economist will know that he I was as "advanced "in his thinking on the Irish question as on almost every other. This, it is pleasing to observe, is made clear, and brought within the knowledge of the masses, in a new "Life of JOHN STUART Mitt," written by Mr. W. L. COMITNRY, the accomplished member for !Cornwall,S. B. It is published, it should be added, by MT. WALTER SCOTT, in his "Great Writers" I series, at the pricy of one shilling. We I commend the volume to readers of all kinds: they will find it full of ideas ; and they will be all the better for a closer acquaintance with a great and good man. It is a well-remembered fact that Mill WM returned to Parliament for 1 Westminster without canvassing for a single vote, or paying a penny towards his election expenses but it is not so well-remembered that while in the !House of Commons he spoke and wrote in favour of Ireland. Mr. Courtney, who is aWm and impartial biographer says His first vote in the , House was in support of an amendment in favour of Ireland, moved by an Irshi member, for which only five English and Scotch votes were given; the other four besides Mill's being those of Mr. Bright, Mr. McLaren, Mr. J. B. Potter, and Mr. Hadfield." Later, in the winter of 1887, he wrote a pamphlet on "England and Ireland" which was very popular, at any rate, in Ireland. Mill himself says :—"The leading features of the pamphlet were, on the one hand, an argument to show the node- nimbleness, for Ireland as well as for England, of separation between the countries, and, on the other, a proposal for settling the land I question by giving to the existing tenants a per- manent tenure, at a fixed rent, to be assessed after due inquiry by the State." The proposal wee scoffed at as Utopian at the time; bet not many years elapsed before the Liberals placed it on the ! statute book; and to-day, in accordance with custom in matters of reform,the Tories try to make their followers believe that the scheme is one which has at all times had their support. It will be the same with Home Ride a few years hence; they will claim that they were always in favour of the ' principle, but not of Mr. GLADSTONE'S Bill. MILL described the Tories as "the stupid party;" and they are dopid—until they make up their minds that the time has come to "jump Jim CROW?' MILL himself has been spoken of by Mr. GLADSTONI as the" Saint of Rationalism," and, adds the great leader of the Liberal party, "he did mi all good." Summing up his influence, Mr. COURTNEY observes —and with this we will conclude—" In logic, in ethics, in politics, we have nourished ourselves at! his springs. Let us make the full acknowledgment of our debt, and also add that, while all that was worst in him belongs to the eighteenth century, all that is best is akin to the highest, best spirit of the nineteenth."

five thousand persons visited the gallery on Sun- day last. There are people, no doubt, who will condemn the practice. It may shock the few, but what of that if it improves the many -- There are ways and ways of ensuing a happynew year. Mr. Balfour's way is to run its" aa many Irish M.P.B as venture to speak out in Ireland. It is estimated that when Parliament meets he will have increased Lord Salisbury's majority by at least eight votes. This is quite an original way of keeping a Government in power, when they are losing caste with the electors.

Mr. Edwin Booth, the American actor, has won money as well as fame on the boards. He is rich, and better still, he is as generous as he is rich. A magnificent new building, standing in Gram- ency Park, Now York, to be called the Players' Club, has been presented by him to the theatrical profession. Well done Edwin ; there are Booths and booths, as players well know.

An English actor of eminence— Mr. Wilson Barrett—does not cut so fine a figure. On New Year's Day, he was fined 25 and costs, at the Leeds Borough Court, for allowing two doors of the Leeds Grand Theatre, of which he is lessee, to: be securely fastened during a performance on the evening of Boxing Day. The law does not permit of play-goers being boxed up in this way —even on Boxing Day. They must have a reasonable chance of escape in case of tire.

Mr. Irving's revival of "Macbeth," at the Lyceum Theatre, seems likely to prove "a palpable hit:' Oddly enough, his performance was dis- counted when he first essayed the part in 18M, with Miss Bateman as "Lady Macbeth." We remember thinking then that it was his finest repreaentation. But somehow he didn't look like a I brow Scotchman, and 'playgoers are too apt to pay attention to the outward appearance rather than the inward reality.
There is a smell of powder in the air. The great Powers of Europe are all preaching peace, but at the some time they are arming to the teeth. Longfellow says, and Longfellow is right:— . .
War,;half the power that tills—inankind with terror, Were half the wealth beatowed on campe and courts, (liven to red em the Intim° mind from error

There were no need of arsenals nor forts. They aredoingsomething "redeem the human mind" in the United States. American philan- thropists have been giving on a grand scale. A London correspondent says The largest bequest 6 the latest, a sum of no less than £'2,400,000 given by Mr. J. V. Williamson, of Philadelphia, for an industrial school and home for boys. The whole of the twelve charities mentioned, only one of which is less than k 90,000, are devoted to the spread of education. This is surely a noble record in the history of any nation." -- Berry, the hangman, is very particular. It is stated that he is about to bring an action for libel against a Kidderminster pressman who reported that the hangman had been holding a levee. But where does the libel come in ? Would it be libel- lous to say the judge held a loves? And are they not both officers of the State? Now, if the reporter had stated that Wily had taken,or given, 1"a drop too Touch" that would have been much more serious. But he didn't, and nobody says anything of the kind.

Yarmers have taken to barbed wire fencing because it is cheap, serviceable, and easily laid. But it is the terror of huntsmen, and they are urg- ing that farmers should take such fencing down. And they will—for a sufficient consideration. Mr. Oakely, the master of the Atheratone hunt, has threatened to resign and leave the district. The farmers have had many losses, and they may sur- vive even this. It is fervently hoped taut, if Mr. Oakely does leave the district, he will not take the land with him.

It was very kind of the Magistrates at the War- rington borough police emu-t, on Monday, to dis- miss the case against the British Workman Public House Company • very kind, but we cannot say that it was cousiatent. When a man pleads guilty, it is generally understood that it is out of the , power of the bench to dismiss a caso, though they ! may make the penalty a nominal one. It is quite a novelty when an offender pleads guilty, to toll him, in effect, that he is mistaken—he is not guilty. But perhaps the novelty held good for the last day I IW only, and that alas! ;has gone for ever.

Sir It tbert Morier has been nailing down a counterfeit. The story has 6)011 circulated in Germany that, whilst he was Charge d'Affaires at Darmstadt, Ito supplied Marshal Basaine' in 11870, with information to be used against the I Germans. Sir Robert has published a letter from the late Marshal flatly contradicting the , fabrication, and adding that, at that time, he did not even know the British diplomatist, Count IHerbert Bismarck has been requested to give the !story a contnelietion in Germany, but the Count somewhat curtly declines to interfere, although his name is mentioned in connection with the circulation of the slander. However, Sir Robert : gets the best of it ; he gives the statement "the he as deep as to the lungs."

div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. By " ARIEL."

That losing passed th;;Ag7 A very merry, dancing, drinking. Lnoaiinn, ninang, and unthinking time the general cry during the week has been "A Happy New Year." That in local life there hare not been any occur- epees of special interest during the past week. r That at last County Council affairs in Runcorn I seem to have settled down, and now that there are two candidates in the field for each division, it will be a case of hard work and victory to the strong- est.
I --That a search through the register of voters has revealed that Inspector O'Donnell's name appears amongst. the wm.nen electors.

That during his term of office in Runcorn be has proved himself anything but an "old woman," and 1 to the Bonifaces of the town, the mention of his name brings up pains and penalties. That the presiding officer will be called upon to decide whether the Inspector can vote unless he appears in a garb similar to those worn by the persons amongst whom lie is classed. That up to the present Mr. E K. Muspratt is the only candidate who has been brought forward to represent Widnes on the County Council, and that, as he in most popular in all parts of the district, it is expected that he will be returned unopposed. That he hopes to enter the Council not as the repre- sentative of a party, but of the whole of the rate- payers of the division. that, if elected, James Handley will make a good representative for Runcorn South on the County Council, and that his address is well worth perusal. That in offering himself for election he does so at the wish of a very large number of the ratepayers of the division.

Roberta touched down to save disaster. Neutral ground woe a scene of operation from the kick off, Tetley doing yeoman service for his side. Evan.s was to the fore with a splendid kick, and heating by Antrobila Barns., and Maasey raised the hopes of the Warrington supporters. Tetley put in a spirited run across the ground, but all to un purge°, for Roberto immediately after saved what appeared a certain chance of scoring. The home backs now passed grandly, and Northend, after trying to run the ball out front over the line, adopted a wise course of touching down. Give-and.take ply followed the drop out, and after a npell of unintermting play at the War- , ringhm quarter flag, Jolley effected the best rim that has , been witnessed on the Warrington ground this season ' ISecuring the oval, he dashed through his opponents until a clear course preeented itself. Here he rounded I the Leeds backs in grand style, until he foend a barrier , in Tetley, but putting in a judicious kick Jolley again raced up, and mooring prassession once more, he planted the leather in • favourable position for goal. Cheer after cheer greeted this fine piece of play, and the only resemblance we ran call to mind waco aimilar try scored , by Jolley in the match at Dewsbilry, when Warrington eo unexpectedly defeated the Yorkshiremen by a goal to a try. Barnes wee called up to take place, anel a loud theer announced that a goal was the renult. Encouraged by this success the " wirepullers" placed up still more ergorously, and Jolley was again to the Bore with a use- , ful kick to the Leeds twenty-five. Still playing pluckily, I the Leeds men could not stop the Warnngtonians from entering their quarters, and after Antrolxis and Speak- man had treated the enthusiaatic assemblage toe nest ! display of passing, Aehton rushed over the line, but through some informality the point was disallowed. This did reit diecourav the Warrington team in the least, for although Northend temporarily relieved the attach, a has pase from Ilamee to Massey placed the home team at their original position. From a pack Antrobite rani. round the pack, and passing to Spatkman he dodged the opposing hacks with precision and secured the second try. Pair Turner made a good bid for goal. Nothing daunted, the Tykes with renewed , exertions forced their way into the Warrington fortress, and after a brilliant dribble by Clayton, Tetlow CAM- pelled Evans to save, which point brought about half then, the telegraph board then reading as follows Warrington, I—t--2: Leeds Parish Chnrch, 0-0-1. After a slight stoppage, Northend resume 4 Fair Turner by a powerful punt placing, the game at I midfield. Berner then threw across to Massey, and an , effort by Antrobus almost ended in a tangible point being sowed. Jolley put in a useful kirk to the bonds line, and Northend only got the oval away when the I odds seemed greatly against him. A free kirk to Leeds relieved their mile, and for a time the Yorkshire men I severely tested the home defence. Fair Turner strove hard to relieve, but the visitor, stuck to their work I manfully, and no headway could be made. Speakman. I however, cleared the Warrington lines, and a fine move- I ment, in which Povey, Dillon, and Anhton came in for notice, found the home team once more attacking. Barnes put in a tricky run, but his pass was erratic,] and Dodworth and Taster placed the game at the War- , rifireton quarters. Leal continued to press, and a tall] kick by Barnes was foiled in its return by the effective tackling powers of Frank Turner and Unsworth. After ' Manley had made his mark, Notthend had a couple of shots at goal, on ono ()erasion experiencing hard lines in net securing a premier point, as the oval struck the I bar, and bounded into play. Towards the elms the Wan ingtoniane swept down nn the Leeds goal, and a ! dashing run by Jolley, whir got over, was disallowed, , which latter point brought a pleasantly-ront.ted game ' ! ton close, Warrington retiring victors by ono goal, one try, and two minors, to leeds Parish Church three minors. , All the home barks passed and ran with excellent jodgment, and all are deserving of a word of praise for their grand display. Roth Jollier and Massey were in fleet-close trim, and of the half backs to award one more praise than another would be an injustice. In the forward division, Poesy, Ashton, Dillon, and Turner were always in the thick. Tetley, Clayton, Roberts, Barrett, and Turner are deeerving of a word of praise for their plucky efforts on the part of Leeds. Leeds: Roberts, back Northend. Tetley, and Barrett, three-quarter tracks; Dodworth and Clayton, half beets; Lumley, Turner, Coupe, Tebbe, Pickles, Tacker, Robinson, Sutcliffe, and Roberts, far- wants. EARI.FIiTOWN.—PIayed at Gorton, on Monday, before 2,000 spectator, Play was very ' even for a Onto, when Jones, for the visitors, got a ' chalice and scored, whilst later on Siddeley mored the ' second goal for the visiting team. Half-time was called with the score—Earloatown, two goals ; Gorton Villa, nil. On crossing over, Bayley scored the first goal for the Villa. Felton and Siddeley then collided, and the former was carried off the field hurt, the game being delayed nearly ten minutes in consequence. A few minutes before tt Time " W. Shaw landed the third point for the visitors, and the game thus melted in a win for Earlestown by three goals to Gorton Villa one goal. EAHLESTOWN V. 0.11013.1.—A match of great local interest woe played on the Mesnos Ground, FArlestown, between these teams, on Saturday, when there was a largo attendance of speetators. Golborne won the toss and played down hill. Siddeley accordingly kicked off, and the ball wan nicely run up by the Shaw,' and Siddeley, when W. Shaw shot in, and Lowe headed though half a minute from the start. Then the game became lively, and Earlestown premed hard, but Casey and Dotson showed strong defence. Even play followed Champion had afterwards to use his hands. Half-time wa.e reached, however with Earlestown leading hyena goal to nil. The second half opened briskly. The visitors looked dangerou.s, but Green and Harrison cleared. Then Earlestown got down, and had twofruitless corners; after which tiolborno transferred matters and equalised, amidst deafening cheers. This fairly put the home team on their mettle, and Smith's position in the Golborne goal was no sinecure. Then Golborne had a free kick, and no sooner had the ball been started than the referee blew his whistle for caseation of hostilities. On lxiing appealed to by the homer umpire he found he ' had made a mistake, as there was just 15 minutes to ' I play. The Golborne team had by this time left the field, I and would not return, and the game had thus to be . abandoned, both teams having scored a goal.

EXECUTION AT NIAITISTONE.—The execution ' took place at Maidstone Gaol on Wednesday morning of William Gower, 18, moulder, and Charles Joseph Dobell, 19, for the [minter of Hensley Cyrus Lawrence, at Tun- ' bridge Wells, on the 20th July last. Lawrence was thee' keeper at the Baltic Sawmills, where Gower was ' employed, and he aroused (tower's enmity by frequently reporting him talc. Gower and his companion Holten plotted to martler Lawrence. They purchased a I revolver, and, drawing lots, it fell to Dobell to commit I the crime. He enticed Lswrenee out, shot him through the head, and escaped. The crime remained undis- covered until October 11, when both culprits, having joined the Salvation Army, confessed the crime. They it ' met their deaths calmly. General Boulanger has (suede manifesto. He says I 1 there is nothing dictatorial in a programme winch demands Constitutional revision by a Constituent i Assembly, and denies that he has deserved blame from the Republic. div.head: FEARFUL MURDER- OF A GIRL NEAR
div.p: FEARFUL MURDER- OF A GIRL NEAR
YEOVIL

On Wednesday, at a village near South Pether- ten, Yeovil, a girl named Davey, about ten years of age, was found murdered. The body Was discovered in a ditch. The girl went on Wednesday monting, [, as was her custom, to fetch milk for the family from a farmhouse about smile from her home. As she did not return at the usual time her parents became alarmed, and the whole family went in search; hut it was not until noon that tidings of the girl could he gained. She was than discovered by her little brother in a ditch, and partly covered with water, in a field about midway between the farmhouse and the child's home. A rope was tied tightly round her neck, and her throat was fear- fully cut. A broken razor was found on the bank near the ditch. The author of the crime is at present unknown, but about live o'clock on Wednes- day evening a strange man was discovered by a bow to be biding in a stable at South Petherton, which is about two miles from the scone of the murder. Ile at once made off, but the police are on his track, and there is every probability that be will be captured. Intense excitement prevails in the neighbourhood. Dr. Walter, of South Petherton, has incomined the body. He found three cuts on the throat, four deep gashes on the back of the neck, and a longitudinal cut on the lower part of the trunk. Death had resulted from strangulation. The inurdererhad evidently imitated the methods of the Whitechapel fiend. The man arrested at Gillingham, Domet, on suspicion of being the murderer gives the name of William Hillier, and states that he is a travelling glazier, and a native of Warwick. Ile can give no. satisfactory account of his movements during tho past fee. days. The distance from the scene of the murder to Gilling- ham is about thirty miles hut he wield have no difficulty in coveting the distance in the time which , elapsed since the commission of the crime.' The superintendent of police in charge of the case, in an interview with a correspondent, says, so far as Im can ascertain, there is an entire absence of motive, and the , murder most have been committed from mere brutality. The presence of the milk can near the spot led to the !theory that the girl walked voluntarily with bee mur- derer from the road, but the police discredit this. Their !theory is tlmt the villain not the girl in the road, threw a mmse over her head and ill:egged her towards the ditch. The more she resisted the tighter the noose was I drawn.

Mr. Wills, on No. 7 section,had written to him to my that there was not half the quantity of lodgers in his huts that they would hold. Ile Mr. Price) did not propose building any more huts at Rixton-yard but he was going to build 20 or 30 more buts at Thelvrall, and should run a "mail " night arid morning for he inen between Thelwell and Riston,as he found that the men had an objection to living at Rixton, on account of the place being so far away from anytown Or railway station. THE ART GALLERY-THE HOUGHTON
COLLEC

Sir,—The MUSPUTII Committe are to be congratulated upon the success of their recent efforts us above referred to. The Pictures, 271 n number, which have been so gener- ously lent by Mr. W. D. Houghton, are of such excell- ence, and at the amne time no varied in character, style, and subject matter, as to mobs up a free exhibiiion ' which is entirely unprecedented in Warrington. It will be a matter for sincere regret if the pr,sest opportunity is not eagerly v)ixed by every one in the neighbourhood who is possessed of the slightest lovefor either Nature or Art. If gratitude is "A lively sense of favours to come," and if our Art Gallery is to le as attractive and useful as its originators intended and wished it be, then those for whose pleasure and insUliction the present " loan" has been arranged, (I mean the public gener- ally) should avail themselves in the largest possible num- bers of the great treat now ready to their hands. A vote of thanks from the Museum Committee, Con- firmed by the Town Cooncil,w.ould not,' feel certain, con- vey to Mr. Houghton ono tittle of the satisfaction which would be his if lie knew that his pictures had been viewed by the thousands of his fellow townsmen. My sole object in writing this letter is to bring as promin- ently as possible before the notice of your readers the ' very keen pleasure whichan inspection of these Pictures will afford to them—bars truly,

WHO PAYS RATES ?"

Sit—Not without mingled surpriseand amu.sement, did I read the simple, evasive, pointless, and vainly attempted abusive letter by "Economist," which appeared in your issue of Dec. 22, 1888. I was surprised because of his repeated persistent nonsense, for lie must know, if enly from the information given to hint in my previous letters, that he is wrong. 'rho statements he at ' first made were as for from the truth as they could possibly be. The only way that I can account for his foolish persistency is that, writing under the name of " Economist," his real name is withheld, and con- sequently, unknown to the public. lam amused because of his constant wriggling, his naturism., attempts to evade the points at issue, and his shifting from statement to statement as all many subterfuges behind which to hide, while his heart swells with vexatton at being no nicely caught, and his object, which has been no apparent in all his letters, exposed. Were " Economist " sensible and well meaning, he would not only acknowledge his mistake, but show gratitude for being corrected and put right, before Im further displays his folly. I hope 'hat the leasons he learns from this correspon- dence may be wholesome. Let lam not forget the words of a wise man, "Meddling with other men's matters, is like taking a dog. by the ear." It is patent that the object of •• Economist" from the first was to delude the working-clas.s, and as many more as possible. Wore this not the ease, Ile would stick to tlie points in question, doing his best to arrive at the truth, with a desire to enlighten others. In that case there would be no necessity for" Faionomist " to hidebehind mysterious sentences, profeesing to have deduced his arguments by scientific laws, ha. What does " Economist " say in his last letter ? It is simply halts column of statements, thrice reiterated, finishing up with something stead wealth, which evidently was not clear to his own mind, even with a couplet to help from Buena. The questions under discussion are, Ist, Who pays rates? 2nd, would the raising, or lowering, or abolishing of rates altogether, affect the property owners and occupiers? and, 3rd, the borough revenue from increased assessments, on old property, and the increased gross , rate collections fmm property built within the last 14 years. My answer lathe first quustion is, that the rates of the borough are paid by either the property owners, or the tenants, or both combined. " Economist " Pap that they are not; but are paid by the owners of the land " This, according to his letter dated Nov. 17th, is" the scientific, answer deduced from a consider- ation of economic principles or laws." That, however, doee not alter the fact that the rates are paid by the owners or occupiers, and certainly no sensible man would ever attempt to prove ,at " Economist " has under- ' taken' win., that land owners pay borough rates. In 1 fact lcannot bring my mind to thmk that "Economist" believes it; b,,t suppose he does, I think that he ought to ' consult some one wiser on thi) subject than hien- ' self. The information may be got from almost every , householder in the town, but certainly from every owner of property, or quarterly, half yearly, or yearly tenants, or If he prefers, let him go to the rate collectors, who , would, I feel sure, willingly give the information If Econoinist " is above humiliating himself in this way to obtain the required knowledge, let Mtn take iny previous advice, and spend £l,OOO it he has it) in the purchase of property, I could then guarantee that he would soon find out his ignorance, especially if he did not reckon the rates with other expenditure teem the gems income. lie would then findthat insteadof getting five per cent., he would get about four. The "scientific answers deduced from a consideration of economic principle or lawn" wont do. 'rhis no one knows better than " Economist," for in his last letter, when trying, 1 but failing, to overthrow my argnments, he closed his first paragraph by saying that he "will leave the reader to 1 find out." Let me state the fact again, which cannot successfully be denied, that the rates of the borough are paid not by the landowner), but by the property owners and occupiers. 2nd, Would the raising, lowering, or abolishing of rates altogether, affect the property owners and occupiers ? I snswer that it would, decidedly, and directly, affect ! them. " Economist" distinctly says that it would not. Let us take his own words see letter dated November 17 " 'rice fact of it is that west all the rates abolished ! to-day. the rimtpayers of Warrington would not benefit by a single penny. The whole benefit I,f the abolition of rates would be enjoyed by that small and, as a rule, very comfortably provided for class who own the ground plots of Warrington." 'this and oil 'notations arecopied from " Economist's "own letters, although he denies it ; in fact, to make up a letter, be repeated the very words in his last of December 22nd. Let toe ask, Did anybody ever talk such nonsense ? It LS worse than childish. Take a case; sum., " Economist" is prepared with, and spends £l,OOO ccc lisporty as follows Five houses at £2OO each, £l,OOO ; producing a gross annual yearly income at £l5 12.5. per house, £7B; ground rent at £1 B.s. per house, £7 ; rates (rateable VAIIIP) ss. 10d. per £ at £2 18s. per house, £l4 105.; repairs at £1 per 11011 SP, £s' emptias at 05. per 11011 Se Ll 10s., nett income. £5O. The above fairly and honestly represents in every particular " Economist's" £l,OOO,
ACCIDENT IN THE FOG NEAR WARRINGTON.

On Thursday evening, William Cann, of lloyle-st., Warnngton, who is employed by Messrs. Carter and Sons, bakers, Bridge-et., was delivering bread in the country when &serious accident befell him. Between six and seven o'clock he was passing along the road which leads through the Dingle at Hill Cliffe when he was compelled, owing to the dark- ness and denseness of the fog, to cautiously lead his horse, sending on before a lad, who accompanied him, with a lamp. Notwithstanding these precau- tione. however, he drew too much to one side, when the van and the horse toppled down a declivity of several feet in depth. Cann falling with them. The van was badly smashed, the bread it contained being scattered in all directions, and at the bottom of the incline the horse lay upon Cann's legs, holding him down in a painful position for a considerable time. The lad, on seeing what had happened, ran to the nearest farmhouse and obtained assistance, Cann being afterwarda conveyed to the Infirmary at War- rington, where it was found that hie injuries were, fortunately, not of a very serious nature, and he was ultimately taken to his home.

with his land taken for 999 ymrs, at a fixed yearfichief rent of £7, producing a nett income of £5O per year, or 5 ,1 percent. on Iris £l,OOO. Now, in this case, suppose the rates were abolished. How, in the first place, could that affect the landowner, since no alteration can prisiibly made in the chief rent during the time specified by agreement? It certainly could not. Then who could he benefited? For the property would then produce a nett income of not £5O per annum, but £B4, being an increase of £l4 previously paid for rates. This must benefit either the owner of the property or the occupier, or both, and would in either case overthrow all "Econo- mist'," erguments. 3rd. I said that the borough grout rate collections have so increased within the not 14 years, that either the rates should be lowered or the ratepayers of the town ought to have extra advantages. " Economist" does not deny that the ratee ought to be lowered, neither don he appear to argue that we have all the advantages we should have. All he has named up to the present is, "That we have a Town Hall, Museum, he., but at the same time he says that whether theou are an exact equivalent for the rates that have been collected and spent is a complex prehlem, which he has not, and will not, attempt to solve. Should " Economist " write again, I hope that ho will keep to the subject under discussion, without so much wandering. Or, feeling that he is right, and for the advantage of the ratepayers generally, would like two or three hours debate on the question, I shall be very happy to meet him, and will indrrrery pay dad- tfie expen.ig, on condition that the meeting shall be froe of charge. By this means "Economist " would be known, and the public would no doubt be satisfied and benefited. HENRY THORNTON.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL. WARRINGTON.
div.p: COUNTY COUNCIL. WARRINGTON.

The Aspect of affairs in regard to the selection of candidates to represent the three divisions of Warrington on the Lancashire County Council has undergone no great change since particulars were given in our last issue. Theonly gentleman who has, so far, been nomi- nated, is Mr. Henry Thornton, insurance manager, the Laurels, Poulton-with-Pearnhead, who is proposed by Mr. James Clare, seconded be Mr. Charles Stullow, and assented to by MMISI.S. Peter i ' llare Charles Rigby, Kever Wait, James Bradshaw, Hugh Ebenezer Hawthorne, Joseph Banifortli, Henry Siddell, and Thomas Shaw. Mr.'rhornton is nominated for the North-East Division. He will, we understand, be an independent candidate, as we are informed that he has severed his connection with the Liberal party, and resigned his psitem as chairman of one of the divisions of the North-East Ward, his complaint being as to the way in which he was treated by the party at the last municipal election. It is understoTal that, in accordance with the decision of the Town Council, Councillor F. Math, J.P., will also : be nomina ed for the north-east division, and that Coils. cillor F. A. Roberts will be nominated for the north-west division. In addition to being the nominee of the Town Council, Councillor Roberts has this week received a requisition largely and influentially signed from the burgesses of the north-west division, desiring him to become a candidate for that division, and pledging themselves to use every legitimate means to secure his return, and Mr. Roberts has expressed his intention of acceding to their request. It is stated that the nomi- nation paper of Mr. John White, as candidate for the third (southern) division, has been filled up, though it had not yesterday been handed in at the Mike of the Town Clerk. Next Monday is the last day on which nominations can be made. WINWICK.

The contest in the Vi inwick division is being carried on very quietly, neither of the two candidates—Mr. J. C. Sutton and Mr. Jam. Warburton—having yet addnissed any public meetings. Yesterday a paper nominating Mr. Sutton was signed by several members of the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority. In this paper Mr. Sutton is described as clerk to the {Carrington Board of Guardians, his residence being given as Heath Dale, Frodsham, Cheshire. He is proposed by the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Beachfield. Glambrook, seconded by Mr. J.. Pennington, Dell Farm. Winwiek, and the assentors are Messrs. Joseph Humphreys, Coerdley ; Wm. Houghton, W.lsten ; Joseph Swinton, Arbury ; John Houghton, Poulton; and Richard Kilshall, Burtonw.d. The paper has yet to be signed by three other gentlemen. It is probable that Mr. Sutton will receive a second nomin- ation.

div.head: DARESBURY DIVISION.- MR. EARP AT HALTON.
div.p: DARESBURY DIVISION.- MR. EARP AT HALTON.

Earn, who had a cordial reception, delivered a speech in which he gave a lurid explanation of the work the Counts Connell would have to perform With regard to his opponents, Mr. Earp pointed out that Mr. Greens!t was an outiiderand a magistrate, argoing that to elect a magistrate was absurd and anomalous. (Applause.) With regard to Mr. Linaker he could no find out how he could represent theist. (Laughter.) ink to become members themselves, and if the ratepayers did not mind, the majority on the Councils would be landlords. A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Charles Lister, li'.. of Auden Hall, for the Lynim Division of the county of Chaster. was held in the brill Hall, on Satur- day evening. Mr. H. It. Dewhurst, of Oughtrington Han, presided. Mr. Lister, in the course of his address, said that in Cheshire there were were 300 bridges under the cognisance of the magistrates, and 580 miles of main roads. The average cast of maintenance in rural districts was about £56 per mile, and in urban districts close to large towns about £l2O per mile, the entire cost of the main roads being no less than £42,000 per annum. This would in future be all repairable by the County Council, and he sincerely hoped they would find means to employ teal labour and that strangers would not be imported to clothe work. (Applause.) The present average cost of county administration in Cheshire, including the police, was about £llO,OOO a year. This would require a Td. rate, but with the river Weaver, payment and repayments from Government, dm, it was reduael to about E 58,000 a year, or a rate of 40., and this met the repayment for the cattle plague loan expiring in 1898. Notwithstanding this, Cheshire wit, one of the lowest, if not the very lowest rated county i i England. (Applause.) In the adjoining county of Lancaster it wan 13d. They dad twit candidates before them, one nominated by the {Farrington Farmors' Club, the other was then addressing them. He did not with to Ray one ' word in disparigetnent of the aims and objects of the Fawners' Club, but before rho. club took upon itself to bring forward eandidatee throughout that district, he ! should ha glad to karn that it was really supported by, and spoke for the farmers. (Applause.) He said li,' was not in the habit of undertaking duties he could not perform, and lie Amid, if his attendances were not satisfactory, be willing to give place to somebody else. His opponent bad been put forward as a farmer or ; farmers' candidate, vet he did not farm a single yard of ! land. Ile i Mr. Lister) was no political eandislate, and never attmirlisl a political meeting in his life.—A resole- ' Goa approving Mr. Lister's candidature was unanimously i adopted.

A young publican, named Frederick Gandy, was thrown from his trap and killed, at Kingston, Dorset, on ' IVednewlay night. Arriturrsu Mostisw—The Glasgow police reported on Thursday that Mary McKenzie, a prostitute, was attacked that morning by a man named Stevenson, who stabbed her ou the neck in seven places. SCHWA IN PUNSTON.-011 Thursday morning a master joiner and beilder of Preston, named Alston, committed suicide by blowing out his brains with a revolver. He had suffered from an incurable complaint for some time and from depression. Ho held a good position.

div.head: ALLEGED SEWING MACHINE SWINDLE AT LYMM.
div.p: ALLEGED SEWING MACHINE SWINDLE AT LYMM.

Mr. Peter Stubs, on Friday week and peeterday, I , was engaged at the Lyman Police Court in mraduct- ing a preliminary investigation into several eavioue Charges against Sarah Cairacross, Annie Ditchlield, and Peter Davies, all of Lyman. Davies, who Is lying very ill, at •house on Rush Green, pleaded guilty, through Sergeant Harrington, to forgery, and, con- jointly with the others, to conspiracy to defraud George Beverley, an engine driver on the Ship (anal, of 30s. Canner°su was further charged with uttering a receipt, , well knowing it to foe forgery, and with obtaining a sew- iJJ g machine, value .£7 2a. Bd., from Jones in 0,04 Man- I cheater and Warrington. div.p: WARRINGTON lsr STARR - BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.

The second annual meeting of the first Warring- ton (826th) Starr-Bowkett Building Society, wan held on Thursday evening, in Legh-,t. schoolroom. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Walker, chair- man of the directors, and amongst those also present were Messrs. Joseph Owen, U. Sutton, Thomas Burton, George Lea, Wm. Crampton, John Griffith, and David Sumner (directors) P. Cramp- ton, Isaac Hayward, Geo. Pillinger, Ilerbert Richards, J. S. llolmes, Miller, S. Carter, D. Martin,' Jas. Colledge, J. Whitehouse, and W. Winetanley ; W. Mallard and F, Pearson (auditors) ; and Jos. Titcliett and Geo. Titchett (secretaries). The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said that I they would remember that at the but annual meeting! the chair was occupied by Mr. Noah Istgge, who, since' then. hail been carried off by the common enemy who would take them all some aay. The directors and the members, too, no doubt, woula feel that they had lost not only a good member of the Society, who set a goof example, but a most excellent chairman. It would be men front Ow balance sheet that they had a good report to make. The Society was in full working condition, and the result was that their expenses were less and their profits were greater. (Hear, beard As a matter of course, for the first year there were always formation expenses to be taken into account. This year they stood in the position of having a profit of £BO In. 4d. upon the working of the society. Last year, being the first, they were not in a position to announce a profit of more than £6 75... that they had made a large advance upon that. (Applause.) They had reason- able hopes that when they- were next railed together at the annual meeting, there would be a still more handsome profit. lie adviosl those present tn see that their balances were correct en the tolance Amt. It was desirable that they should check them, though Inc did not suppose that, after the cam ful au Ming, there would be any mistakes. Ice might meation that although the society was complete onto, MI the number of members was concerned, it was open for those who liked to take up further share.. Some members had not more than two shame, and the rules admitted of any single member holding four shares in one book. They had a total of 1,185 shares, but the full permissible number of shares was 1,006. Of mum, it rested with any of the members, if they thought things were going to mend—and he hoped they would have a prosperoirs and happy new year—if they wanted to add to their savings in that direction, to incr.. their number of sham to four. Mr. Titehett (secre- tary) occasionally had enquiries act,, whether members had books to sell. Ile did not mention that by way of suggesting that anyone should part with books, but in order to show that in what they might call the money market of the town there were enquiries ni such a character, indicating that the society had a stable foot- ing, and that it was mognised as a good, solid invest- ment. A second society that had been formed in Warrington wan making go. progress. Up to now it had got ntembers, and shares had been taken up. even more rapidly, he believel, than was the case with the first society. Altogether there were now in this country getting on to a thousand aoeioticu of that character. More than 100, he thought, had been formol sinn'e their society came Otto existence. The general report was that they were making steady and geed progmx, and that they were proving a great boon to the community. Many of them would be acquainted with ordinary build- ing societies, which lod been prosperous. in prosperous times, but which, unfortunately fur the members, had in bad times resulted in a great deal of money being hot. The basis of a Starr-Rowkett Society was such that no risk of that kind was incums]. So for as invest- ments were made, they were individual invest- inents, and the society could not pos,ibly lose by anything of that kind. The savings of the working and middle classes were very hardly got together, and the first element of such savings should be that they were absolutely safe. 'flier.. was no such thing as alsolute safety in the strictest smoe of the word, but, after care- ful observation of that society and of others, he has] coma to the conclusion that it was as safe nail was tms- sible for any society to be. (Applause.) Mr. J. Titehett then road the report and bahnce sheet. 'lle report stated that the total income,. front all sources, for the year ending November 3rd, 1888, amounted to £1,474 10s.
