div.head: RAILWAY COLLISION ON THE RUNCORN
div.p: RAILWAY COLLISION ON THE RUNCORN

In consequenceof some mistake in the telephonic signalling yesterday morning, a locomotive started from Acton Orangent the same tune as a locomotive left , Runcorn. Attached to the Acton engine was a saloon carriage containing Mr. John Walker, nephew of the eon- tractor, who is agent of the Moore section, and on , ! the Runcorn engine were a number of foremen. The ! engines met some distance below the trestle bridge at , the Big Field, but fortunately they were proceeding slowly in consequenee of the heavy fog that prevniled, I ! and the collision had not those serious results that might • I otherwise have occurred. The force of the concussion was not sufficient to dislodge the engines front the metals but they were considerably damaged, and every pane of glans in the saloon was shivered to atoms. Mr. Edwards, a foremen, when he saw the collision imminent, jumped from the engine, and escaped with a slight bruise on the knee. Mr. Walker luckily escaped without a scratch. The walking ganger, Mr. Shelley, was pitched from the engine down the steep embankment that occurs at the place, and he wan very fortunate to be able to scramble up, having only suffered a slight shock. The quarry foreman, Mr. Wnght, was note. fortunate. He waa sitting on the coal bunker when the collision took place, and he was thrown violently forward, his head coming in contact with the ironwork. Ile sustained rather serious injuries, and he was at once conveyed to the surgery of Dr. McDougall, who paid him every attention. The drivers and stokers of the locomotives were slightly shaken.

THELWALL, LYMM. fist. Operations at Thelwall and Latchford are almost at a standstill owing to the frost and other causes. Two steam navvies+ near the Hospital are at work, but other- wise the cutting presents rather a deserted appearance. On the Lyinm section also the work has been proceeding very quietly during the last few days. Last week closed with a flood, muilting from the heave and continuous rain, but the contractor hail learned 'Wisdom from expe- rience, and protected himself all round by substantial embankments, which effectually kept out the water. Means for drawing off the water, for which the farmers in days gone by, when the spring and summer rains inundated their meadow lands, called out in vain, are now in me, for the water is now run off in a night, and the flood can be lowered a yard almost in an hour. The brickyard is kept in full operation, and a large I ptantity : of muff excellent bricks is being stacked for use here- after on the works.

div.head: MAGISTRATES AND THE COUNTY COUNCILS. BY • CHESHIRE ELECTOR.
div.p: MAGISTRATES AND THE COUNTY COUNCILS. BY • CHESHIRE ELECTOR.

During the present id:Wei:infers of the Electoral Divisions of the County of Chester will be called upon for the first time to exercise the Fran- chise in the election of County Councillors, and it is much to be wished that every ratepayer, whether male or female, will feel that his or her duty requires the exercise of this privilege, as it is a matter which touches the whole community, especially that of the poor. The new Local Govern- ment Bill gives to the ratepayers the right to manage the affairs of the County in which they resole. The opportunity has been given, but it rests with the individual to use, abuse, or neglect the gift. Those who allow a County Council to be elected without taking their proper share in deter- mining its constitution can only blame themselves if their intereets are neglested in the proceedings of the Council for the next three yeare, and it must be remembered that before this time hut elapsed the jurisdiction of the Council may be indefinitely increased. Thus the importance of the forthcom- ing contests must be judged, not by the terms of the present Act, but by the possible development into i which it may soon expand. ! In looking over the names from many and various lona of the Kingdom, it would seem that peers, magi.- ' tratm, landlords, and landlord's agents, are likely to ! form the main part of the new bodies, as they did the ! whole of the old. This in not as it should be. Business communitim must be represented by business men, , farmers must be represented by some one whit is inde- pendent of landlords' favours, and communities of working-men 1111 l stbe represented by men whoseinteresta are identical with their own, who live in their midst, who are readily accessible, and who know the peculiar ' wants of the constituency. Many good candidates have come forward to contest the various Cheshire electoral divisions, and, let it be added, many utterly unsuitable candidates. With- out going far from home, take for instance the Runcorn Union, where five magistrates are seeking the suffrages of the electors. Under the old system of county govern- ment, the magistratm (a body a gentlemen over which ratepayers have no control), bad sole management of the , financial and judimal affairs of the county, and it was felt, and justly so, that this state of affairs could not he continued in jmtice to the ratepayers. The new ! lecal Government Act, which has now become law, places in the hands of the County Council, a body of !men elected by the ratepayers, the control of the countfs finances, leaving to the magistrates the justiriary affairs. It ion well known fact that magistrates looked withdisfavour upon this arrangement, and made serious opposition to the passage of the Bill through Parliament, hut without any large amount of sucrose. Now, evi- dently with the intention of nullifying these (to them) obnoxious provisions, they are seeking seats in the Council, and should they be suctmurful in their amulida- hoe the new Act becomes a dead letter. Ratepayers should remember that if magistrates are really dmirous of helping to work the Act successfuny, they can do alas magistrates, as the Act provider for the County Council and Magistracy consulting together. In the Darestaury Division of Runcorn, which includes the parishes of Halton, Weston, Preston Brook, Norton, Moore, Aston, Sutton. and Dutton, three candidates are in the field. Mr. Edward tires-null, of Grappenhall, magistrate, Mr. H. Linaker of Frodsham, a landlord's agent, and Mr. William Richard Earp, of Creston Brook, tanner and chemical manufacturer. It is difficult for a personmther than oneof exceptional obliquity of vision, to see what claims the two former gentlemen have upon Cite constituency, what large proportion of the ems- munity they will represent, if indeed any part, or why the electors of the division should be asked to return in the person of a magistrate a repnwentative of a class whose object is to revert to the old state of things and nractieally Kerr:try-him the ratepayers ; or to return a landlonl's agent who knows notlting of the wants of the working classes and tnulesinen. On the other hand, the claims of Mr. Earp seem to be remarkably strong and well-founded. In the first plate he is the rally one of the three who resides in the division, and consequently the only one who ill be ill the midst of those whose interest he is to represent. He is himself a large ratstisYM.nd as employer of lalmur in thn constituency, a man of liberal education and of sound business alsilitim, and is sure to have a knowledge of the difficulties connected with the woehingelaoseo, farniem, and tradesmen. It is to he hopril that every voter. he he tradesman, farmer, or workingman, will rarefully nwtl Mr. Earp's addrms before he promises either venahally or in writing his vote to any of the raiiiiiiiatrs. And so with other constitu- ! coves ; let the eitalors see to it that the opportunity , which is offered Owns is not thrown away, as it will he t mif they do not retuen en of public spirit, and of liberal mind.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTE DIVISION OF RUNCORN. LADINs AND GENTLEMEN,— I have bad the honour of being asked. by a numeronsly-siguel Requisition. tvpresetitlng all shades of religious and political feeling. to offer myself as a Candidate tor your suffrages at the sponnehing Election of County Councillors. In seceding to this request, I vIA it to be understal that I offer me services quite imie. pendently of all political and religious opinions. Being a Large ratepayer, my interests are identical with your own therefore It will be my oarrie.t wish (if elected) to represent, to fhe best ot my ability, the whole (A the Electors of this Division. I am of opinion that the Act under which the County C anvils will he constitute' it a wise ATM prudent measure, and that It was conceived in a liberal spirit. inasmuch as it ail) enable the electors, through their representatives, to exercise a control. which they lave not hitherto posse4sed, mer an important section of their load affairs. and thereby to ensure that due regard for economy whiCh I deem m essential in the administration of public business Should it he your pleasure to elect toe, I will do my utmost to protect your Interests, and advance the prosperity of this important Division. I am. Ladies and Gentlemen. Yours faithfully, C, W. HAZLEHURST.

COUNTY COUNCIL. TO TILE ELECTORS OF THE WIDNES DIVI- SION. LA Dim use Gmert.rwax.—Having been requested by the Local Besot to consent to be nominated as a candidate at the forthcoming election ef the Lancashire County Council, I have much pleasure in placing my services at the disposal of the ratepayers. The Quarter Sessions, liming been invested by the local Government Act with the power to determine the Electoral Divitilol39 of the Catinty.have. in the face of the direct instruc- tion to secure as (Sear possible equal population for each Division, given to Widnes, with a population of nearly 30,000, only one member, while other Divisions with less than 8.000 population are accorded the some representation. An appeal to the Local Government Board to remedy this grievous wrong has been fruitless, and if elected I shall con alder It my trot rioty to take such step, as may be deemed advisable to secure adequate representation for this popu- lous and growing district. Imperial party politics should be excluded from the County Councils. and I believe the ratepayers of Widnes desire that , they should not enter into the election of • representative. I trust this feedtig will continue, and I hope to enter the Council not ace representative of • party, but of the whole of the ratepayers of the Division.—Yours faithfully. K. K. MUSPRATT. Widnes, Dec. 28. 1838.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF RUNCORN, SOUTH Loreono Garytenay.--Slnce the withdniwal of Mr. Brundrit's candidature for your Division (which to me is • matter of very great regret). I have again been urged to offer ran It as a candidate to represent you on the County Council, and, laving been &soured that this is the general wish of the electors, I have inuch pleasure in placing ray services at their disposal. The Local Govemment Act has created an entirely nrw hody In melt county In Broth:id and Wales, which will be stibject to periodical elven., and to which will be entrusted the management of the whninistrative and financial business of , the County. The Land Government Board are alsoempowered Ito make,from time t thne, provisional order.] for transferring to CoutityCounclls, powers and dully, relating to County, !matters, which are now discharged by certain Government , departments. It will be Goon from this bare outline of the duties to he performed by the now Council, that a goal deal of time and attention will have lo be git-en by the member you choose as your representative. If you do me the honour to elect me both shall he willingly placed al your service. During the time I lave been a magistrate. I lave made It • practice to attend Quarter Sessions for the purpose of making myself conversant with the routine of county business. After the passing of the Parliamentary Redistribution Act, I served on the Conintitt, appointed to form new polling districts for the Northwich Division. and the dividing of Runcorn Into two parts, which was then effotted, has in my opinion materially as•isted in seatiring two representative• for the town on the County Council. If it Is your pleasure that I should Pwrn one of the new Council. it shall be my constant endeavour to wee you faithfully. I beg to remain. Your obedient servant, JAMES HANDLEY. Runcorn, December 201 h, 1828.
